n: In this lecture we will talk about the forensic medical examination of physical evidence, and then about the basics of criminal law and defects in medical care. First, the concept of physical evidence. According to Article 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, physical evidence is an object with physical features whose origin, relevance, use or the factors acting on it can be established. It includes the instrument of the crime, objects that have preserved traces of the crime, and objects that were the target of criminal acts. A separate group is biological physical evidence: parts of tissues, secretions such as blood, saliva, urine, sweat, semen and faeces, their stains, and hairs.

t: Who examines, and the place of the clinician
n: Now, who carries out the examination. The examination of biological evidence is conducted by special specialists in the forensic biology, forensic histology, medical criminalistics and forensic chemistry laboratories. The forensic medical examination of physical evidence is not assigned to clinician doctors. In some cases, however, general practitioners may be involved in examining the scene, finding and describing physical evidence and taking samples. That is, the examination is carried out by laboratory specialists, while the doctor helps in finding and collecting the evidence.

On the appearances of bloodstains. Bloodstains may be found at the scene, on the body, clothing and shoes of the victim and the accused, and on the weapon. With heavy blood loss, or on a material with low absorbency, a pool of blood forms, while on a well-absorbing material an absorbed stain forms. On an inclined surface, stains in the form of runs appear. Sliding leaves smears, and contact without sliding leaves imprints. Thus the shape of the stain shows on what surface and by what movement the blood fell.

Now blood drop stains. A drop falling from a height of 10-15 cm onto a horizontal surface forms a round stain with smooth edges. If it falls from a moving part of the body or onto an inclined surface, the stain is pear-shaped, like an exclamation mark, and the narrow side points in the direction of movement. If the height is great, the edge of the stain is finely serrated and splashes appear around it. Splashes are also formed by a sharp swing or by spurting from a large artery.

Rules for collecting bloodstains. The collection of physical evidence, including bloodstains, from the scene is carried out by the investigator; doctors are involved if necessary. Small objects are taken whole. From a large item, the stained piece and a clean piece for control are cut out. From a hard surface, a dry scraping of blood is taken. A sample from a pool of blood is taken into a vial in a quantity of not less than 10 ml. Stains in snow are melted, and a stain on soil or sand is taken to its full depth.

In blood examination, questions are resolved in a definite sequence: first the presence of blood, then species, then group, and finally the particular person. Remember: presumptive tests are nonspecific. Presumptive methods include the benzidine, peroxide, luminol and phenolphthalein tests, as well as ultraviolet light. Thus such a test allows only a presumption of the presence of blood; other methods are needed for a reliable conclusion.

t: Establishing the presence of blood and species origin
n: Establishing the presence of blood and species origin. Reliable methods of detecting blood: microscopic, microcrystalline, spectral and chromatographic. At present the chromatographic method is mainly used reliably. Species origin is established by the Chistovich-Uhlenhuth precipitin reaction, electrophoresis, the Ouchterlony method and others. Separately, the ABAcard test determines in one step the presence of blood in a stain and that it is human.

t: Group origin of blood and attribution to a person
n: Group origin of blood and attribution to a person. There are erythrocyte, serum, leukocyte and enzyme group systems. The examination usually begins with the ABO system. In forensic medical examination, both agglutinogens and agglutinins of the ABO system are studied. Attribution of blood to a particular person has recently been established strictly by DNA examination. That is, group systems narrow the circle, and DNA points to the person.

t: Blood: sex, region, age and pregnancy
n: On sex, age and other features from a bloodstain. Sex is resolved by determining X and Y chromatin or by DNA examination. In adults the haemoglobin is HbA, in newborns HbF; HbF is more resistant to alkaline denaturation. However, in a stain 15-20 days old they cannot be distinguished. Pregnancy cannot be strictly determined from a bloodstain. Also, about 210 g of dry residue remains from 1 litre of liquid blood.

Semen stains and their collection. Semen stains are examined in the forensic biology department in the examination of sexual crimes and some sexual conditions. The stains have map-like edges, the stiffness of starch. On dark fabric they look whitish, on light fabric yellowish, and when mixed with blood they turn pink. Samples of blood and saliva are taken from suspects and from the victim. Before saliva is taken the mouth is rinsed, then 2-3 ml is collected.

Establishing the presence of semen. Presumptive methods: the potato juice reaction and pale blue fluorescence in ultraviolet light. The Florence and Barberio reactions have no practical importance. Reliable methods are morphological and chromatographic. In the morphological method, finding even a single whole spermatozoon, that is, head, body and tail, is considered a positive result. In azoospermia and necrospermia, paper chromatography is used: if choline, spermine and acid phosphatase are found together, the presence of semen is reliable.

Secretor status and other secretions. In about 80 % of people, group antigens are found in secretions, that is, in semen, urine, bile, saliva and faeces; such people are called "secretors". The presence of saliva is established by the enzyme amylase, of sweat by the amino acid serine, and of urine by creatinine and urea. Faeces are detected under microscopic examination by food remains, microorganisms and helminth eggs. Remember: the species origin of urine and faeces is not determined.

Storage and dispatch of samples. Objects for examination are dried at room temperature, away from sunlight and from sources of heat, in conditions excluding access by insects, and sent. Each object is wrapped separately. The object under examination and the control object cannot be in one package. When collecting objects from the scene, rubber gloves are worn, and small objects are taken with forceps.

Examining hair: sample and questions. Hair is examined in homicide, sexual crime, bodily injury and road traffic accidents. It is taken with forceps and placed in a separate packet from each region. The comparison sample is taken from five regions of the head, that is, frontal, parietal, two temporal and occipital: a bundle of 20-30 hairs is cut close to the skin. The questions are as follows: whether the fibre is hair, whether it is human or animal, group and regional origin, whether it fell out by itself or was pulled out, type of action, and attribution to a particular person.

How human and animal hair are distinguished. In humans the cuticle has small, dense scales, while in animals it is large, sometimes saw-like, with long scales. In humans the cortex is wider than the medulla. In animals, the medulla occupies the main thickness. That is, the structure of the cuticle and the ratio of cortex to medulla help to distinguish human hair from animal hair.

t: Hair: region, damage and attribution to a person
n: Hair: region, damage and attribution to a person. The thickness of scalp hair is up to 0.1 mm, eyebrows and eyelashes 0.11-0.12 mm, beard and moustache 0.15-0.17 mm. At a temperature above 200 °C hair is carbonised. The cut made by a sharp object is smooth, while from a blunt object the shaft is crushed and splits into fibres. A pulled-out hair has a bulb and remnants of the sheath. Attribution to a person is resolved in probabilistic form.

Forensic histological examination. In all cases where a body has been examined, pieces of internal organs and tissues must be taken for forensic histological examination. Putrefaction and other post-mortem changes cannot be grounds for refusing the examination. Preparations are in all cases stained with haematoxylin and eosin. If necessary, selective staining, frozen sections, fluorescence and polarisation microscopy are used.

t: Forensic histological examination: diatoms and archive
n: Another aspect of forensic histological examination is diatoms and the archive. In the forensic histology department, on the question of entering water alive or dead, diatom plankton is examined; water samples are also submitted. The result is set out in a report, which consists of an introduction, the examination, the forensic histological diagnosis and a conclusion. The primary, that is, formalin, archive of the body's organs and tissues is kept for not less than 2 years, and the preparations and blocks for not less than 3 years.

Medical criminalistic examinations. In the medical criminalistics department, diagnostic, identification and situational tasks are resolved. Types of examination: trace (trasological), ballistic, identification, micrological and situational. The main aim of the trace examination is to determine the injuring factor from the injury or marks. The ballistic examination is carried out in firearm injuries and blast trauma: the number of injuries, the sequence of shots, the distance, and the type of weapon and projectile are determined.

Identification, micrological and situational examination. The identification examination establishes whether a body or remains of an unknown person belong to a particular person; at the last stage a conclusion on identity is drawn. From skeletal remains, species, number of bodies, race, sex, approximate age, stature, diseases and injuries are determined. The micrological examination studies the transfer of micro-traces and microparticles. The situational examination studies the possibility of carrying out a certain action.

Forensic chemical examinations. The forensic chemical examination is conducted to confirm or exclude the presence of toxic substances or their derivatives in biological objects. The tasks: detecting and quantitatively determining toxicologically significant substances, identifying drugs and narcotics, interpreting the results, and analysing non-biological evidence. In a toxicological examination, at least two methods of different principle are recommended where possible. Archive objects are kept in alcohol in a refrigerator for up to one year.

Now the concept of crime. The features of crime: danger to society, criminal unlawfulness, guilt and punishability. In the Criminal Code, a crime is a guilty, socially dangerous act, that is, an action or omission, prohibited under threat of punishment; this is Article 14 of the Criminal Code. A socially dangerous act causes harm to the objects protected by the Code or creates a real threat of harm.

Forms of guilt: intent. For guilt, the act must have been committed under the control of consciousness and will; a person is found guilty of committing an act intentionally or through negligence; this is Article 20 of the Criminal Code. In direct intent, the person foresaw the consequences and desired them to occur. In indirect intent, he consciously allowed the consequences; this is Article 21 of the Criminal Code. Crimes committed with direct intent are not characteristic of the work of medical workers. Criminal abortion and official forgery belong to such crimes.

Forms of guilt: negligence. In overconfidence, the person foresaw the possibility of consequences occurring, but groundlessly hoped they would not occur; this is Article 22 of the Criminal Code. In carelessness, the person did not foresee the consequences, but should and could have foreseen them. In practice, in most cases medical workers are held liable for crimes committed through negligence.

Two examples of negligence. The first example: carrying out an elective operation without reason, without preparation and without assistants: this is overconfidence. The second example: the doctor did not know the standards and a complication led to death: this is carelessness. That is, in the first case the person acted while denying the danger, and in the second ignorance of the standard led to the consequence.

Extreme necessity. In extreme necessity, if the danger cannot be averted by other measures and the harm caused is less than the harm prevented, the act is not a crime; this is Article 38 of the Criminal Code. Example: outside an institution, in laryngospasm, a tracheostomy was made with improvised means. The patient's life was saved, and a purulent complication followed. Such an action by a doctor cannot be assessed as a crime.

Justified risk. If an action corresponds to modern scientific knowledge, the aim cannot be achieved without risk and harm is prevented, the risk is considered justified; this is Article 41 of the Criminal Code. In justified risk, even if a socially useful result is not achieved, no liability for harm arises. Exception: a risk taken in the knowledge of the danger of people dying is not recognised as justified.

t: Difficulty of establishing the medical worker's guilt
n: The difficulty of establishing the guilt of a medical worker. Let us give an example: in a district hospital, a patient with a cardiac injury, there are no special facilities, transfer and calling a specialist are impossible. The surgeon on duty sutured the cardiac wound. This decision creates a certain danger to life, but it was the only correct one. The professional risk was justified, and the act is not a crime. Thus establishing the guilt of a medical worker is a particularly complex case for the judicial and investigating bodies.

t: Grounds for ordering a commission examination
n: Grounds for ordering a commission examination. The ground is a resolution of the inquiry officer, investigator or prosecutor, or a ruling of the court. The descriptive part of the resolution states the circumstances of the case, then the type of examination and to whom it is ordered. In the operative part, the questions are put. The questions must be precise, clear and not go beyond the competence of the commission of experts.

Documents submitted to the commission. The case materials, medical documents and objects necessary for the examination are submitted to the commission. An examination on the basis of separate extracts from the case history and certificates is not permitted. The reference on the employee being held liable and departmental inquiries are also submitted. In case of death, the conclusion on the body or the pathological record is required.

t: Composition of the commission of experts
n: Composition of the commission of experts. A commission examination is conducted only in forensic medical examination bureaux; the commission consists of not fewer than three people. Heads of the institution where the event under discussion occurred, and persons interested in the outcome, cannot be members. The lead expert, rapporteur and members have equal procedural rights and duties. This means that in the commission no one's vote prevails.

t: Assessment of the conclusion and questioning
n: Assessment of the conclusion and questioning. Participants cannot attend the commission's meeting and the stage of drawing up findings. Members of the commission can be questioned only on the existing conclusion, after it has been submitted. Under Article 187 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the conclusion is assessed together with other evidence and does not have prevailing force.

Basic concepts. A patient is a person who has sought medical care, irrespective of whether there is a disease. Quality of medical care is a set of features showing the conformity of care with modern science and standards. A medical standard is an ordered sequence of the volume and character of treatment and diagnostic measures. These three concepts form the basis of the next topic.

The concept of DMC. A defect in medical care, that is, DMC, is not a legal concept. In a broad sense it is failure to follow, or improper following of, generally accepted rules, instructions and regulations; a condition that led or could have led to an adverse outcome. From the standpoint of criminal law, only defects that caused an adverse outcome in a causal link are taken into account.

t: Four groups of defects by essence
n: Four groups of defects by essence. By the essence of the defect, that is, the content of the shortcoming allowed, four groups are distinguished. The groups: diagnostic, treatment, preventive and other defects. For example, in diagnosis there is late diagnosis, in treatment incorrect use of a medicine, in prevention violation of sanitary rules, in the others an error in record-keeping.

Defects of diagnosis and treatment. Defects of diagnosis include failure to identify the underlying disease or injury or its complication, and failure to identify an important concomitant disease. Defects of treatment: late hospitalisation, shortcomings in surgical treatment, errors in prescribing and carrying out medical procedures, irrational management of labour. Incorrect use of medicines and other defects of treatment also belong to this group.

The three stages of DMC by place. By the place where the defect was allowed, three groups are distinguished: the pre-hospital stage, the hospital stage and other institutions. The pre-hospital stage includes the rural medical post and the polyclinic. The hospital stage includes the district hospital and the maternity department. For other institutions, the sanatorium and the children's home are examples.

Causes of DMC. Causes are the circumstances that brought it about; they are conventionally divided into three groups: subjective, organisational and objective causes. Subjective causes include inattention and insufficient qualification. Organisational causes include absence of means and shortcomings of organisation. Objective causes include late presentation and atypical course.

t: Effect on outcome and causal link
n: Effect on outcome and causal link. In criminal law the presence of an outcome as a result of the defect is very important, so the effect on outcome is studied separately. DMC may lengthen the treatment period, affect disability or death; sometimes, however, it has no effect on the outcome at all. Remember: only a direct causal link is a ground for holding a doctor liable.

The "doctor's defensive attitude". The risk of an adverse outcome sometimes prompts a doctor to carry out medical procedures in a minimal volume; this is called a "defensive attitude". In foreign literature it is called "defensive medicine". It is hard to identify: for this, medical documents and materials on the subjective side of the offence are studied.

The assessment algorithm consists of three stages. The algorithm requires the analysis of DMC to be carried out in a definite sequence. First, the patient's pathology. Second, assessment of the doctor's actions. Third, the causal link between action and outcome. When the analysis is carried out in this order, the conclusion is consistent.

t: Three variants of effect on outcome
n: Three variants of effect on outcome. The first variant: the pathology developed naturally and DMC had no effect; in this case there is no causal link. The second variant: DMC worsened the condition or created a predisposition; in this case the link is indirect. The third variant: DMC led to a new pathological process; in this case the link is of 3 kinds, which in the table are given as direct or indirect.
